item.title: Coefficient Giving just gave GiveWell $1 billion. Where should other donors give now?
item.description:
Published on July 24, 2026 3:37 PM GMT

Linkpost for my Substack piece, lightly adapted. Disagreement very welcome.

What happened

Coefficient Giving (cG) announced a $1 billion gift to GiveWell on 23rd July. This increases a previous commitment of $175m for 2026. cG say this could be a one-off surge, but it has implications for other donors either way. Both organisations have lowered their funding thresholds this year (GiveWell from 8x their benchmark to 6x, Coefficient from 2,000x their benchmark to 1,000x). Even if GiveWell hit their aim of grantmaking that will "approach or even exceed $1 billion this year", cG's gift is roughly the size of everything GiveWell expects to grant this year.

They don't specifically mention AI wealth, but I think it's fairly clear what they mean when they say "much of the future funding we're anticipating depends on the valuations of some extremely volatile assets." They also say that a belief in the potential of AI to transform global health affects their decision. In essence, AI wealth and short AI timelines are now setting budgets for bednets, vitamin-A distribution and vaccination incentives. This is the first major example of how the Funding Anthropalypse will reshape EA.

What should donors do - my take

The answer depends on size. For donors giving thousands, not much has changed: 6x GiveWell's benchmark is still some of the best marginal cost-effectiveness a normal donor can buy, and GiveWell has committed to tell donors if it thinks their money should go elsewhere. If you are giving thousands each year, I would stay as you are.

For donors giving millions, a lot has changed. The highest impact move is probably not adding to GiveWell's margin, but building other capacity that will help to absorb next year's likely windfall. cG concede that "the marginal cost-effectiveness of GiveWell-directed funding will be lower than it has been in the past couple of years", and that donors redirecting marginal donations would be, to some degree, "perfectly rational".

Finally, this does nothing for power concentration - if anything, it makes it worse. cG and GiveWell are the two largest players in EA, and they are not independent: the two largest funders are now exposed to the same volatile source at the same time. I expect the gift itself to be an outstanding grant at the object level, funding highly cost-effective programmes that do an enormous amount of good for very little money. But this excellent grant does nothing to address the fragile architecture of the space.

Disclosure: I have a conflict of interest in some of what I recommend in the full piece, as an operator in this space myself via the Mid-stage Global Health Fund. Discount accordingly.

A few things I'd be interested in hearing about:

  • If you're setting a seven-figure giving budget for 2026 this week, does this news change it?
  • Is "build absorption capacity" actually tractable for an individual large donor, or does it fall apart on contact with the pipeline?
  • How worried should we be about two interdependent funders, versus just glad about $1bn of excellent grants?

item.title: The Long (Self-)Correction
item.description:
Published on July 24, 2026 9:01 PM GMT

I propose the Long Self-Correction[1] as an alternative name/idea/concept to AI Pause and Long Reflection.

Problem with AI Pause: Pause until when, and for what purpose? Presumably to make AI (that we'll build later) safer, but the deeper problem is that humans aren't safe, and can't safely serve as builders, overseers, or alignment targets for powerful AIs.

Problem with Long Reflection: It seems to imply that the main problem with humans is that we just haven't had enough time to think, that reflection is the main thing we need to do more of, and then we can get on with building powerful AIs or other technologies. Or that if we build aligned AIs that sincerely help us think a lot more, or do the thinking for us, then things will turn out fine.

So I think we need a catchy handle for a related but distinct idea, that humans aren't ready to build AIs or other extremely powerful technologies, because we're currently too flawed, in a variety of ways, and it will take a long process (which may or may not end up succeeding) to fix those flaws.

A summary of the flaws that I have in mind:

  1. not having a workable moral framework (consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics all having serious problems)
  2. being bad at philosophy and long-horizon strategy
  3. being badly calibrated about our philosophical and strategic competence, i.e., not realizing that we're incompetent, despite overwhelming evidence (see e.g. FTX and early MIRI, and many others, trying to maximize impact while assuming their own philosophical and strategic competence)
  4. in practice, human morality is a kind of status game that actively disvalues careful strategy and philosophy in most places
  5. positional/zero-sum values (like power and social status) being a huge part of human motivations, but almost nobody explicitly reasons/talks about this while discussing, for example, AI safety or effective altruism or how to make the long term future turn out well[2] 
  6. being easy to manipulate (or go off-rails by oneself) via things like sycophancy, plausible-sounding philosophical arguments (see e.g. Objectivism or Dialectical Materialism), limerence, hero worship, spirituality
  7. not understanding the nature of philosophy so that we don't know how to go about fixing many of these issues even in principle
  8. not realizing how flawed humans are, or the full scope and interlocking nature of the human and AI safety problems, and thus being prone to over-optimistically proposing or implementing partial solutions (e.g., thinking that making AIs aligned or corrigible to humans or to some favorite moral theory would be sufficient to make them safe, or that we just need the right people to win the AI race, or Tool AI, or Scientist AI)

(This list focuses on key bottlenecks that seem hard to fix even with AI assistance or intelligence enhancement, and isn't meant to be a complete list of human flaws / safety problems. It ignores e.g. that the median human is ignorant of many important issues, and that we're currently quite bad at complex large-scale coordination such as passing/implementing close-to-optimal government policies.)

My main hope for a Long Self-Correction eventually succeeding rests on the fact that humans have seemingly, mysteriously, made progress on these issues over a very long period of time, so if we preserve the environment in which we can seemingly do this, and not give anyone or anything the power to permanently derail such progress, then maybe we can continue to snowball The Correction until we reach a point when we can rightly justify reshaping the universe according to our volition.

  1. ^

    It will probably be shortened to "The Long Correction" at some point if it catches on, similar to how "outer space" is now often just "space".

  2. ^

    Why isn't there a version of EA that explicitly talks about how to leverage people's status motivations to do more good for the world? It's very possible that explicit talk about status is actually counterproductive at least in the short run, e.g. it heightens status motivations and makes people less altruistic, but then do we just march into the future while blindfolding ourselves to this aspect of human nature?

item.title: Amsterdam Insect Protest
item.description:
Published on July 25, 2026 11:10 PM GMT

(Please share with your friends in the Netherlands).

On August 5, in Amsterdam in the Netherlands, there’s a protest that could help shut down the world’s largest insect farm. It’s at Teleportboulevard 105 1043 EJ Amsterdam, Netherlands. Read more at this link. There’s also a zoom call on Wednesday 29th July at 12:30pm (CEST) with more info. This is a super important protest, so if you’re in the Netherlands, please show up!

This single farm, Protix, raises tens of billions of farmed insects. Shutting down this farm could affect many hundreds of billions of insects in total. The life of a farmed insect is a nightmare: the adults are not fed and left to starve to death; the juveniles are shredded, boiled, or microwaved; they’re overcrowded so that disease spreads rapidly and natural behaviors are thwarted. There aren’t any welfare regulations for insects.

If larger animals were being treated this way, we’d all recognize it as a horror. But the fact that insects are small shouldn’t make much difference to how bad their mistreatment is. So long as they can suffer, we shouldn’t cause extreme suffering to trillions of them for no reason. It is pretty plausible that black soldier flies (the kind Protix farms) feel pain. Amos Wollen nicely summarized the evidence:

To date, the best and biggest literature review is Gibbons et al.’s 2022 paper, “Can insects feel pain? A review of the neural and behavioural evidence”, which reviews over 350 articles. Gibbons and her co-conspirators considered the evidence for insect sentience along eight criteria: nociception, sensory integration, integrated nociception, analgesia, motivational trade-offs, flexible self-protection, associative learning, and analgesia preference.

While there was, in many cases, a paucity of evidence—shame, shame!—there was, apparently, no good evidence that any insect failed on any of the eight criteria.

Protix is strapped for cash, but they might get bailed out by their current investors like InvestNL—an investment fund dependent on taxpayer funding. If you’re a Dutch taxpayer, your tax money might facilitate the painful slaugter of billions of insects. This protest would gently encourage them not to bail out Protix :).

Investment also makes little financial sense. The industry claimed it would transform the food system and has failed completely. Companies are imploding left and right, but investors are still investing. There’s just no viable path forward: farmed insects are more expensive, worse for the environment, and pose greater pathogenic risks than alternatives. A Dutch newspaper summarizes the dismal state of the industry in a piece titled How Investors Completely Choked on Edible Insects. And Protix has failed to answer basic questions about how their product could become remotely viable.

Even if you don’t think insects matter much morally, we shouldn’t harm them by the billions without a good reason. The insect farming industry has no good reason to exist. It has failed at delivering each one of its foundational promises. There is no reason to keep sacrificing billions of insects to provide exorbitantly priced environmentally harmful petfood and food for farmed fish.

If we assume that each person at the protest adds an extra .01% chance of shutting down Protix, that Protix’s continued operation will lead to an extra 300 billion farmed insects, then each protestor benefits an expected 30 million insects. It’s not every day that you have the option to benefit a population 10% as large as America! If you’re in the Netherlands, Belgium, or West Germany, go to the protest and take a friend. If you’re not, send this to your friends in those areas. This really, really matters.

In justifying starving black soldier flies to death, the industry often claims that they don’t have mouths to eat. This is false, like much of what the industry says. But though they have mouths, they cannot speak—there is no one to represent the starved, crushed, boiled, and ground-up black soldier flies who rot in overcrowded indoor facilities. Join the protest to stop this senseless cruelty and protect those who have no voice.

item.title: $1 billion grant to GiveWell: How Might This Change Who Gets Funded?
item.description:
Published on July 25, 2026 7:10 AM GMT

On Thursday, Coefficient Giving announced a $1 billion commitment to GiveWell. I expect it to be a superb grant, funding interventions that are about as cost-effective as anything we know of. It will likely improve, if not save, millions of lives whilst also building the capacity of both GiveWell and recipient organisations for the future. 

But it feels like more than a single grant. Coefficient were clear that this is "a one-off surge, not a new steady state", and that they are moving now to build capacity ahead of a much bigger wave of giving they expect in the coming years (GiveWell's own note on the commitment is here). Set that against the AI IPOs on the horizon and the windfall so many are anticipating (the "third wave" of American philanthropy) it is hard not to read this as the opening salvo in what may turn out to be a seismic shift in how global health and development gets funded.

None of this is new as a topic of conversation; plenty of folks have been talking about it for a while and there plenty of articles on the EA Forum itself discussing much of what I have laid out, frankly more eloquently. But it appears that it is now actually arriving, and I find I have a lot of feelings about it. I wanted to set them down honestly if nothing else, to concretize my own thoughts. 

The Clear and Positive Case

Let me start with what I think is unambiguously good.

Highly cost-effective, evidence-based interventions may now have the funding they need to reach dramatically more people and improve their lives. With the collapse of USAID and the wider retreat of multilateral funding over the last two years, there is a real and painful gap for exactly the sort of interventions that are rigorous, cheap, and deserving of support. A billion dollars, deployed well, means more children sleeping under bed nets, more supplements reaching those who need them, more nutritious food, more unconditional transfers to people living in poverty. In the near term, this will help a very large number of people. This is great! 

Additionally, the thing I deeply appreciate about GiveWell, whether or not you share their giving philosophy, is their commitment to radical transparency, to red teaming, and openness to feedback on their methodologies and calculations. These values give me, and hopefully the wider community, some comfort that they are bringing a growth mindset to their grantmaking rather than treating their models as settled truth. It is a large part of why I hold my fears and uncertainties somewhat weakly. 

Concentrations of Funding

Jack Lewars has written cogently on his Funding Anthropalypse Substack about the risks of concentration. His core worry, which I largely share, is that when funds concentrate within a single funder operating from a single mindset, you lose diversification - and with it, you introduce the risk of a single methodological or philosophical error propagating through the whole system. Perhaps a fairer way to put it is not "error" but a systematic underweighting of a certain kind of giving, such that some interventions end up over-invested and others under-invested. This seems highly plausible to me, and I think the value of worldview and funding diversification is real.

Jack has covered the equilibrium of giving better than I could. I want to look at a different equilibrium ...

The Equilibrium of Implementation

The thesis: A funder's ability to disburse money well is operationally constrained. Nick Allardice, President and CEO of GiveDirectly, has made a version of this point well: a historic wave of money may be about to arrive, and the sector simply is not built to absorb it at the effectiveness and scale this moment demands. The capacity to move money well is itself a binding constraint. There are only so many grants a single person or team can make, and this is especially true for funders that hold the line on rigour, transparency, red teaming, and cost-effectiveness - values I admire and believe are core to impact, but which are slow and expensive to staff for. 

The natural consequence is an incentive towards larger grants, disbursed more quickly, particularly for a funder without an endowment to draw down gradually, as is essentially the case with GiveWell (as I understand it). 

GiveWell themselves are incredibly transparent in this, as they note, “Our researchers are explicitly searching for bigger opportunities than we’ve had the resources to investigate and to fund in the past. … Our growing team is investigating promising programs at a scale we haven’t previously been able to pursue.” As I read this, I understand this to infer that the organisations best placed to absorb a step-change in philanthropic capital quickly are the large multinationals and BINGOs (big international NGOs) that already have the operational, legal, and financial machinery in place around the world. They can take in significant sums fast, because the scaffolding already exists.

I want to be careful here. I see nothing intrinsically wrong with the interventions these organisations deliver, and while there are critiques of the BINGO model, that is not my argument. My argument is that if a wall of money flows preferentially to the largest and most easily-fundable organisations, we may quietly lose something that matters a great deal. 

What’s the Matter with Individually Great Grant Making at a Larger Scale? 

In the short term, more of the same feels fundamentally positive – millions of lives will improve. My concern is with the medium and longer term, and it runs along three lines.

What I worry about most is underinvestment and potential loss of innovation and nimbleness. The organisations working at the edges - locally-led organisations, new entrepreneurs coming out of Ambitious Impact Programs and similar incubation programs, and people simply experimenting - are the ones least able to access this kind of resource, and they are precisely the ones a creative non-profit landscape needs. This is the both/and I keep returning to: the sector is both extraordinarily effective and frustratingly conservative, depending on where you look, and it needs the big absorptive players and the small experimental ones. More of the same will not change the overall vector of global development. Changing that vector takes thousands of entrepreneurs trying thousands of interventions, most of which will fail, a few of which will be the next bed net (or wheat flour fortification … sorry, my bias kicked in).

Next, the implications on the labour market. A concentration of capital in the largest organisations will pull talent toward the players who can pay the most. Labour movement is sticky, so once people move, they tend to stay. It will also drive up salaries, which I actually think is a good thing: so many of us in global health and development are, frankly, underpaid and running on intrinsic motivation, and a correction there is overdue. However, this can also calcify talent within certain types of organisations, pricing out smaller (read as more likely to be innovative) organisations that may deserve to scale. 

Finally I am concerned with a loss of M&E rigour, and it is the one closest to my own work. A large and fast influx of capital puts pressure on the very epistemics that make cost-effective giving cost-effective in the first place. It is worth saying plainly, as I have argued before, that a potentially highly cost-effective intervention on paper is not the same thing as a cost-effectively implemented one, as we have seen with Dispensers for Safe Water. The modelled figure and the realised impact on the ground can diverge sharply, and the only way to know is to monitor implementation fidelity and hold on to a healthy scepticism about whether the money is actually doing what the model says it should. Given the enormous opportunity cost of these potentially larger grants, that discipline matters even more.

This kind of monitoring is neither cheap nor quick, and I think that can be under-appreciated. Take the area I know best, anaemia reduction. Testing implementation fidelity at the beneficiary level is time-consuming, and the core indicators of whether anaemia is actually falling - haemoglobin and serum ferritin - can take up to twelve months to shift in a way you can validly measure and attribute to fortification. Good monitoring and evaluation often takes time, and if the dominant incentive is to move money quickly, that is precisely the sort of slow, unglamorous rigour that can get squeezed or alternatively shift away from interventions that are simply too time-consuming to monitor and evaluate.

What might help

None of this is an argument against the grant. To Coefficient Giving's real credit, this $1 billion appears squarely focused on building absorptive capacity - both GiveWell's own, and that of the key recipients it funds. What I fear is that we end up building the absorptive capacity of only a subset of the sector. It is, without doubt, a highly impactful subset and one that can reach huge numbers of people. But it may leave underweighted exactly the players who could drive the innovation and creativity we will need over the long term. So this becomes an argument for pairing the grant with deliberate investment in absorptive capacity further down the pipeline. A few mechanisms seem worth serious consideration:

  • Ring-fencing a portion of funds for smaller and medium-sized organisations, explicitly accepting that the cost-effectiveness of funder time will be lower for these grants or regranting. This is a real cost, and I think it may be worth paying. Ultra Philanthropy (as one example) appears to be doing exactly this and could serve as a highly effective hedge to the risks I have laid out.
  • Investing in operational scaffolding so that smaller organisations can scale and absorb funding without building every function (particularly operationa functions) from scratch. Scaling fellowships are one route (similar to Mulago Fellowships, 100x, and The Nudge Accelerator) focused on organisations implementing evidence-based, highly cost-effective interventions. Secondary or shared-service organisations are another - Health Progress Hub, Impact Ops, High Impact Professionals, Consultants for Impact, and others in this space can meaningfully reduce the operational burden of scaling.
  • Funding nimbler monitoring and evaluation that can generate credible evidence for uncertain innovations on shorter timelines. A/B testing, robust internally run M&E frameworks: systems that support evidence that arrives fast enough to actually steer an experimenting organisation towards cost-effective impact.

The common thread is that the highest-leverage use of some of this money may not be another large grant to a proven recipient, but investment in the capacity of others to become fundable at all.

Closing

I think this is the start of a catalytic moment: an opportunity to lift billions of lives and to sustain the innovation and nimbleness the sector will need for the problems that come after. I feel real gratitude for the generosity and foresight of the individuals behind this, and I am confident their giving will improve an enormous number of lives.

Given the deep uncertainties of the medium and long term, though - including AI's own implications for wealth, labor, and the shape of economic development - I think a little caution is warranted. My sense is that the right posture is to welcome this wholeheartedly while protecting worldview diversification and working actively to minimize the risks of concentration in who may be delivering interventions.

I am far from certain about any of this, and I would love to hear where others think I have got it wrong.

Coefficient were clear that this is "a one-off surge, not a new steady state", and that they are moving now to build capacity ahead of a much bigger wave of giving they expect in the coming years (GiveWell's own note on the commitment is here). Set that against the AI IPOs on the horizon and the windfall so many are anticipating (the "third wave" of American philanthropy) it is hard not to read this as the opening salvo in what may turn out to be a seismic shift in how global health and development gets funded.

None of this is new as a topic of conversation; plenty of folks have been talking about it for a while and there plenty of articles on the EA Forum itself discussing much of what I have laid out, frankly more eloquently. But it appears that it is now actually arriving, and I find I have a lot of feelings about it. I wanted to set them down honestly if nothing else, to concretize my own thoughts. 

The Clear and Positive Case

Let me start with what I think is unambiguously good.

Highly cost-effective, evidence-based interventions may now have the funding they need to reach dramatically more people and improve their lives. With the collapse of USAID and the wider retreat of multilateral funding over the last two years, there is a real and painful gap for exactly the sort of interventions that are rigorous, cheap, and deserving of support. A billion dollars, deployed well, means more children sleeping under bed nets, more supplements reaching those who need them, more nutritious food, more unconditional transfers to people living in poverty. In the near term, this will help a very large number of people. This is great! 

Additionally, the thing I deeply appreciate about GiveWell, whether or not you share their giving philosophy, is their commitment to radical transparency, to red teaming, and openness to feedback on their methodologies and calculations. These values give me, and hopefully the wider community, some comfort that they are bringing a growth mindset to their grantmaking rather than treating their models as settled truth. It is a large part of why I hold my fears and uncertainties somewhat weakly. 

Concentrations of Funding

Jack Lewars has written cogently on his Funding Anthropalypse Substack about the risks of concentration. His core worry, which I largely share, is that when funds concentrate within a single funder operating from a single mindset, you lose diversification - and with it, you introduce the risk of a single methodological or philosophical error propagating through the whole system. Perhaps a fairer way to put it is not "error" but a systematic underweighting of a certain kind of giving, such that some interventions end up over-invested and others under-invested. This seems highly plausible to me, and I think the value of worldview and funding diversification is real.

Jack has covered the equilibrium of giving better than I could. I want to look at a different equilibrium ...

The Equilibrium of Implementation

The thesis: A funder's ability to disburse money well is operationally constrained. Nick Allardice, President and CEO of GiveDirectly, has made a version of this point well: a historic wave of money may be about to arrive, and the sector simply is not built to absorb it at the effectiveness and scale this moment demands. The capacity to move money well is itself a binding constraint. There are only so many grants a single person or team can make, and this is especially true for funders that hold the line on rigour, transparency, red teaming, and cost-effectiveness - values I admire and believe are core to impact, but which are slow and expensive to staff for. 

The natural consequence is an incentive towards larger grants, disbursed more quickly, particularly for a funder without an endowment to draw down gradually, as is essentially the case with GiveWell (as I understand it). 

GiveWell themselves are incredibly transparent in this, as they note, “Our researchers are explicitly searching for bigger opportunities than we’ve had the resources to investigate and to fund in the past. … Our growing team is investigating promising programs at a scale we haven’t previously been able to pursue.” As I read this, I understand this to infer that the organisations best placed to absorb a step-change in philanthropic capital quickly are the large multinationals and BINGOs (big international NGOs) that already have the operational, legal, and financial machinery in place around the world. They can take in significant sums fast, because the scaffolding already exists.

I want to be careful here. I see nothing intrinsically wrong with the interventions these organisations deliver, and while there are critiques of the BINGO model, that is not my argument. My argument is that if a wall of money flows preferentially to the largest and most easily-fundable organisations, we may quietly lose something that matters a great deal. 

What’s the Matter with Individually Great Grant Making at a Larger Scale? 

In the short term, more of the same feels fundamentally positive – millions of lives will improve. My concern is with the medium and longer term, and it runs along three lines.

What I worry about most is underinvestment and potential loss of innovation and nimbleness. The organisations working at the edges - locally-led organisations, new entrepreneurs coming out of Ambitious Impact Programs and similar incubation programs, and people simply experimenting - are the ones least able to access this kind of resource, and they are precisely the ones a creative non-profit landscape needs. This is the both/and I keep returning to: the sector is both extraordinarily effective and frustratingly conservative, depending on where you look, and it needs the big absorptive players and the small experimental ones. More of the same will not change the overall vector of global development. Changing that vector takes thousands of entrepreneurs trying thousands of interventions, most of which will fail, a few of which will be the next bed net (or wheat flour fortification … sorry, my bias kicked in).

Next, the implications on the labour market. A concentration of capital in the largest organisations will pull talent toward the players who can pay the most. Labour movement is sticky, so once people move, they tend to stay. It will also drive up salaries, which I actually think is a good thing: so many of us in global health and development are, frankly, underpaid and running on intrinsic motivation, and a correction there is overdue. However, this can also calcify talent within certain types of organisations, pricing out smaller (read as more likely to be innovative) organisations that may deserve to scale. 

Finally I am concerned with a loss of M&E rigour, and it is the one closest to my own work. A large and fast influx of capital puts pressure on the very epistemics that make cost-effective giving cost-effective in the first place. It is worth saying plainly, as I have argued before, that a potentially highly cost-effective intervention on paper is not the same thing as a cost-effectively implemented one, as we have seen with Dispensers for Safe Water. The modelled figure and the realised impact on the ground can diverge sharply, and the only way to know is to monitor implementation fidelity and hold on to a healthy scepticism about whether the money is actually doing what the model says it should. Given the enormous opportunity cost of these potentially larger grants, that discipline matters even more.

This kind of monitoring is neither cheap nor quick, and I think that can be under-appreciated. Take the area I know best, anaemia reduction. Testing implementation fidelity at the beneficiary level is time-consuming, and the core indicators of whether anaemia is actually falling - haemoglobin and serum ferritin - can take up to twelve months to shift in a way you can validly measure and attribute to fortification. Good monitoring and evaluation often takes time, and if the dominant incentive is to move money quickly, that is precisely the sort of slow, unglamorous rigour that can get squeezed or alternatively shift away from interventions that are simply too time-consuming to monitor and evaluate.

What might help

None of this is an argument against the grant. To Coefficient Giving's real credit, this $1 billion appears squarely focused on building absorptive capacity - both GiveWell's own, and that of the key recipients it funds. What I fear is that we end up building the absorptive capacity of only a subset of the sector. It is, without doubt, a highly impactful subset and one that can reach huge numbers of people. But it may leave underweighted exactly the players who could drive the innovation and creativity we will need over the long term. So this becomes an argument for pairing the grant with deliberate investment in absorptive capacity further down the pipeline. A few mechanisms seem worth serious consideration:

  • Ring-fencing a portion of funds for smaller and medium-sized organisations, explicitly accepting that the cost-effectiveness of funder time will be lower for these grants or regranting. This is a real cost, and I think it may be worth paying. Ultra Philanthropy (as one example) appears to be doing exactly this and could serve as a highly effective hedge to the risks I have laid out.
  • Investing in operational scaffolding so that smaller organisations can scale and absorb funding without building every function (particularly operationa functions) from scratch. Scaling fellowships are one route (similar to Mulago Fellowships, 100x, and The Nudge Accelerator) focused on organisations implementing evidence-based, highly cost-effective interventions. Secondary or shared-service organisations are another - Health Progress Hub, Impact Ops, High Impact Professionals, Consultants for Impact, and others in this space can meaningfully reduce the operational burden of scaling.
  • Funding nimbler monitoring and evaluation that can generate credible evidence for uncertain innovations on shorter timelines. A/B testing, robust internally run M&E frameworks: systems that support evidence that arrives fast enough to actually steer an experimenting organisation towards cost-effective impact.

The common thread is that the highest-leverage use of some of this money may not be another large grant to a proven recipient, but investment in the capacity of others to become fundable at all.

Closing

I think this is the start of a catalytic moment: an opportunity to lift billions of lives and to sustain the innovation and nimbleness the sector will need for the problems that come after. I feel real gratitude for the generosity and foresight of the individuals behind this, and I am confident their giving will improve an enormous number of lives.

Given the deep uncertainties of the medium and long term, though - including AI's own implications for wealth, labor, and the shape of economic development - I think a little caution is warranted. My sense is that the right posture is to welcome this wholeheartedly while protecting worldview diversification and working actively to minimize the risks of concentration in who may be delivering interventions.

I am far from certain about any of this, and I would love to hear where others think I have got it wrong.

item.title: Job: Executive Director of CEEALAR (EA Hotel)
item.description:
Published on July 26, 2026 5:24 PM GMT

TL;DR: We're hiring an Executive Director to lead CEEALAR through its most ambitious phase yet. Beyond running our existing Blackpool hotel, you'll plan and spearhead our expansion into London, including its fundraising and staffing. This is a project that is designed to 10-20x our impact. We need someone who can be both a reliable custodian of what exists and a driving leader of what comes next. Full-time, £40,000-£50,000 (with significantly more contingent on successfully fundraising and expanding into London), UK-based (Skilled Worker visa available), rolling applications until 31st August 2026.

Looking for your next high-impact role?

We are looking for a highly dynamic and strategic individual to lead CEEALAR's growth. There is considerable flexibility for the candidate to shape the role according to their own strengths and preferences. We envisage this being a full-time role. As our current operations are in Blackpool, we expect a short (1-3 month) stint of living and working on-site in Blackpool to get detailed knowledge of the inner workings of the organization. If a grant for a London expansion is approved, we expect the location to shift significantly toward London, including moving to London (with a few days spent in Blackpool each month).

What you'll do

  • Planning and spearheading CEEALAR's expansion to London, a new location intended to 10-20x our impact, including leading its fundraising and staffing from the ground up.
  • Acting as custodian of our existing Blackpool hotel while building and leading the new London operation: developing and directing CEEALAR's overall strategy and growth, including impact measurement.
  • Overseeing finances across both sites, including developing budgets, improving our accounting system, running payroll, and preparing annual reports for the Charity Commission.
  • Securing funding for the charity, including writing grant applications and diversifying our funding streams, with the London expansion as a central fundraising priority.
  • Acting as spokesperson for the charity, including writing articles about CEEALAR and representing it at wider EA events.
  • Leading our small and growing team, including line managing our Operations and Community Managers, interacting with the Board of Trustees, and overseeing recruitment across both locations.
  • Ensuring CEEALAR adheres to all laws and regulations, for example, HR, hospitality, and charity law.

Person specification

We recognise that we are asking for a diversity of competencies and encourage people who have even one of the concrete skills to apply. The job can be somewhat adapted to the skills of the successful candidate.

  • A strong understanding of, and passion for, CEEALAR's mission, as well as for effective altruism more broadly.
  • 3+ years of relevant experience (in the form, please note how your experience is relevant to the role).
  • Demonstrated ability to fundraise, ideally both within EA circles and with UK grantors, a core requirement given the scale of the London raise.
  • A strong strategic mind, with the ability to scope, plan, and deliver a major expansion while running day-to-day operations across sites.
  • A good team leader, able to motivate and develop others, and to build a new team from scratch.
  • Excellent verbal and written communication skills.
  • The ability to problem-solve and navigate challenges with persistence and positivity.
  • Experience of any of the following is desirable. Alternatively, the proven ability to learn these types of competencies quickly would be valuable:
    • Pre-opening experience (launching a new hotel, venue, or site)
    • Budgeting and accounting
    • Leading a small and growing organisation in the charity/impact space
    • Fundraising
    • Law and governance in the charity sector
    • Hospitality management

Compensation and benefits

  • A salary of £40,000–£50,000 (with more (including much more) potentially available after the first successful fundraising), pro rata, depending on experience. For exceptional candidates, further negotiation is possible.
  • 5.6 weeks paid holiday per year.
  • Flexible working hours (you can set your own hours).
  • £1,000 annual equipment and training budget.
  • We can provide a UK Skilled Worker visa if needed.
  • Accommodation and food are provided in Blackpool if you live there.

Application process

Our application process is quick:

  • You fill in this short form. Deadline: 31st August 2026, EOD UK time. Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis, and early applications will receive an advantage.
  • Shortlisted candidates will be interviewed by our team via video call (possibly preceded by a short written work trial, depending on the level of interest in the role).
  • We aim for you to start work on 14th September 2026.

item.title: Moving on from the EA Forum
item.description:
Published on July 27, 2026 3:16 PM GMT

Hello Forum friends! I'm posting today to let you know that I recently left CEA to join 80,000 Hours, as a product engineer on the Career Services Team.

This means I'm no longer running the Online Team, the EA Forum, and the moderation team. I've handed the Forum and mod team to @Toby Tremlett🔹, and @Rory Fenton is leading the Online Team on an interim basis.

I sat on this draft for a while. I've been at CEA for almost 5 years and it's been a wild ride — there's a lot I could write about! I didn't want to keep putting it off, so just a warning that this post is a bit disorganized. Feel free to ask me questions if there's anything you'd like to hear more about. :)

A bit about the Forum

It's been a little over a year since my last update post, where I hinted that the CEA Online Team was spending less capacity on the Forum over time and you'd get less updates as a consequence. I estimate that the team is spending a bit over 1.5 FTE on the Forum in 2026, so that trend has continued, and may decrease more depending on whether CEA decides to backfill any of my capacity.

Working on the Forum has been both fun and challenging. I love the idea of the Forum being the best online space to discuss how to do good better, and being a model of EA thinking. Reading the Forum has been an invaluable part of my EA journey (especially as someone whose in-person community is not very EA), and I've heard many similar accounts from others (maybe even you personally! I've talked with many Forum users over the years). I felt so lucky that I got to come into work every day and do something to help such wonderful people who genuinely care about doing good. Plus, it's been inspiring to see how much the people working on the Forum Team over the years truly care about it — the Forum is key community infrastructure and a lot of thought gets put into changes.

I've also found the reality to be more complicated than my ideals. For example, one of the key metrics we track is engagement, and I feel sad that drama is both the highest driver of engagement and leads to the lowest quality comment sections. As engagement was declining following the FTX bump, I was surprised by how little the technical work we did seemed to move the needle, even things that seemed like sure bets such as varying the Frontpage algorithm "speed" based on how frequently the user visited the site.  Although the core Forum product doesn't change much over time, the people using it and the world around it change pretty noticeably year over year, and I worry we've been too slow to respond. The laissez-faire community management of 2021 no longer feels like a good fit today, as I no longer trust the community itself to be good at self-correcting.

Since I took over the team around 2 years ago, I grappled with the question of what to do with the Forum: how much to continue investing in it, and how to position it within (or outside of) a CEA that was quite different from the one that I joined. It seemed to me that our focus should be on the content side — we needed to have a more consistent stream of good quality content, primarily from a small group of strong contributors, and that was key to driving all the other value the Forum provides. This vision didn't quite fit in with CEA's goals at the time, and so we ended up focusing on growth and significantly reducing the capacity spent on the Forum.

More on the past 12 months

2025

I ran the Online Team in accordance with CEA's 2025-26 strategy, and most of our work was focused on growth[1].

I spent an absurd number of hours in Q4 2025 writing a funding proposal doc, so allow me a few moments to brag about what we accomplished:

  • Prevented a continued decline in engagement with the EA Forum even while significantly cutting resources allocated to the program (~5 FTE → ~2 FTE)

  • Generated sustained growth in the EA Newsletter for the first time since 2022, and in mid-2025 surpassed 60K subscribers for the first time in its history

  • Revamped the EA Opportunities Board and moved it over to effectivealtruism.org, where it's regularly the top viewed page on the site (see chart below for past 90 days)

    • Plus we recently added full-time roles, which helped us hit our annual 2026 P0 growth goal before the end of Q2

I started off 2025 expecting us to focus on EA Forum community building, and we ended up instead shifting to focus on growth. I personally feel mixed about this:

  1. I'm really proud of my team for hitting all the 2025 growth goals that we set. It's quite satisfying to be able to quantitatively express the outcomes of our work! :)
  2. Increasing the number of people working on EA causes can certainly be good and impactful. I was excited to work on Forum features to help more people get involved with EA when I first joined CEA, and I still think there is a lot of potential to make those more effective.
  3. I think it makes sense to focus on the "put it into practice" half of effective altruism (which is what growth feeds into) if you feel that the "figure out how to do the most good" half is healthy, but I don't personally feel convinced that it's healthy.
  4. CEA cares about not goodharting growth. However, my personal experience strayed closer to this than I was comfortable with.
  5. For the Forum in particular, growth does not currently feel like the right goal to be backchaining from. It's clear that there are tradeoffs between tending the garden and aiming to grow the number of Forum users by X% each year.
    1. For example, I feel convinced that we should implement the rejected content feature that LessWrong built a few years ago. In the short term this will reduce the number of users posting on the site. In the long term this may or may not increase the number of users on the site. Personally, I would be happier with a smaller and healthier Forum community than a larger one that is more like the rest of the internet.

2026

In 2026, we have not been focusing on growth (outside of the EA Opportunities Board). @Toby Tremlett🔹 and I used our Forum capacity to explore directions for the Forum that we were most excited about and felt could be most impactful. It's been interesting seeing some relevant discussions on the Forum! :)

A lot of what's written in the above posts resonates with me. (For example, I think an ideas-first framework fits the Forum better than a careers-first framework. CEA measures talent growth via careers.) Toby and I have been honing in on a more focused direction for the Forum in the ideas space. I'm excited about it, and I'll let him say more about it when he's ready! Plus, from my recent conversations at CEA, I expect that CEA's strategy from 2027 onward will start to cover the "figure out how to do the most good" half of effective altruism[2], which makes me personally more optimistic about its future.

On the tech side, we've mostly focused on setting better foundations by moving to a new codebase. I've been enjoying the new post page more than I expected! I love the new font and it just looks a lot more polished to me. You can read more in @Ollie Etherington's post: EA Forum Update: Migrating to a new codebase.

Thank you! 💙

Huge thanks to the Online Team who helped me run the Forum (@Toby Tremlett🔹 @Ollie Etherington @Agnes Hasselblad 🔸 @Will Howard🔹), to the Forum moderators and facilitators who take care of the space (@JP Addison🔸 @Will Aldred @Francis @Dane Valerie @OscarD🔸), and to all the Forum users who have supported us over this time — this job has been really meaningful for me and I couldn't have done it without all of you.

  1. ^

    For our own products at least. About half of our capacity (design & engineering) goes toward supporting other teams at CEA, which I won't cover in this post.

  2. ^

    To clarify a common misunderstanding: I don't mean that CEA should be doing research themselves, but something more akin to ensuring that the process of figuring out how to do the most good continues, or even improves over time.

item.title: Never born, then maybe died twice
item.description:
Published on July 28, 2026 11:43 AM GMT

“Your balls are baked aren’t they, mate”.

He would not have been born

Thanks Lyndon[1], that describes the situation. Like almost 1 in 10 modern men, my sperm weren’t up to the task - at least not the old fashioned way. So IVF it was - the miracle that now feels almost commonplace.

We landed on the moon and Woodstock changed music forever. But in 1969 a quieter event transformed the world. The first human embryo was fertilised “In vitro”, outside the body. Yet 10 years passed before one was inserted into a womb, and then born. 48 years ago, Louise Joy Brown was the first woman born through IVF. This year about a million babies will be born through IVF.

IVF stands at the frontier of rich-privilege, a norm for the middle class in rich countries. In my home country New Zealand, the government even pays for it! Yet every week I meet women here in Northern Uganda who can’t have kids, and could never afford IVF. Even the human “right” to have a kid can depend on where you are born.

If I was born 25 years ago, or in Uganda, my boy would never have been.


Our Risky Choice

We decided to give birth in Lacor Hospital, the best hospital here in Northern Uganda and where I worked as a doc 15 years ago. If you’re wondering, yes this was risky. While we judged the hospital would be safe for my wife, should something go wrong and our boy needed the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), he would be less likely to die in New Zealand. By my rough calculations, perhaps three times less likely. Even a good Ugandan hospital is far worse than one in New Zealand, for a few reasons
Prematurity: Better hospitals keep more premature babies alive. If born between 24 and 30 weeks, our boy would be twice as likely to survive in New Zealand, compared to where we gave birth.
 

  1. Infections. Basic infection control just isn’t as good compared to a high-income NICU. Parents enter the NICU here en-masse to feed their kids and spread bugs around. Super-bugs aren’t tested for. Hands are less-washed. Cutting-edge antibiotics aren’t available. Our boy would be more likely both to catch an infection and then die from it.
     
  2. Fewer staff and stuff. Fewer nurses and doctors, and less high-tech machines mean that problems will be diagnosed and treated later and more mistakes made. Despite staff’s best effort, kids just can’t be monitored and cared for with the same intensity in Northern Uganda as they can in New Zealand.

Months before birth, a couple of people told us “you’re mad to put your child at more risk”. This may be true, but despite the, overall risk seemed low-ish after a seamless pregnancy. We wanted to give birth close to our home of 13 years, in relationship and solidarity with our community. And we had the Lacor Hospital A team on the case, with a dedicated gynecologist and midwife. But despite our wonderful medical teams’ best efforts, things didn’t go as planned. 
 

He didn’t die once - a routine miracle

“His head isn’t moving” are not words you want to hear. Our boy’s head made it through the cervix, then he got stuck completely. No maneuver, nor three scary suction attempts could move out poor boy past that liminal space between the safety of the womb and our wild world. My wife suffered, our midwife sweated, fear set in.

In most times and places in human history, this would have been the end. For our baby, or for my wife, or for both. But we were in the right place at the right time, with a life-saving procedure just a theatre away.

We thank the Roman innovators who first cut babies from dead lifegiving mothers. We thank the farmer Jacob Nufer, who in 1500 used his experience from pigs to first save both his wife and their  baby. We thank Fransour Rousset, who proposed enfantement caesarien as a routine life-saving surgery. From the 1800s we thank Morton (ether) and Simpson (chloroform) for safer and less painful surgery. We thank Semmelweis for clean hands and Lister for antiseptics. Max Sanger who first decided to actually stitch the uterus closed. And Landsteiner and Fleming for blood transfusions and antibiotics.



We recognise your contribution to saving over 50 million mothers and babies[2].

Even in one of the poorest countries, I didn’t doubt our surgeon’s safe scalpel. Humanity’s stacked innovations have made this miracle almost routine.

Our boy was safely born.
 

He didn’t die twice - Neonatal care

After the exhilaration of holding our boy for the first time, things weren’t as they should be. Our boy didn’t feed properly, became lethargic and turned a bit yellow. One doctor’s assessment was enough to confirm our fears. He was jaundiced and had a fever - he might have the dreaded neonatal sepsis. 

We were fortunate to occupy one of the four private rooms in maternity, with running water, electricity and two beds - luxuries the 20 other NICU families did not have. Every 2 hours as we moved to the NICU to feed him, we tiptoed through and over mothers and families who lined the corridor. I was overwhelmed with guilt from two angles. First that we paid $30 a day without thought for a private room while others slept on the floor. And guilt at our decision not to give birth in New Zealand, where our boy would be more likely to live. Guilt at our immense privilege, and guilt that we hadn’t used it to the max.
 


Over the next 10 days yet another wonderful set of innovations helped him pull through. Our resource poor NICU was still equipped with the most important life-saving interventions, and kept our boy warm, well monitored and infection free.

In 1880, Dr. Tarnier noticed that Paris zoo’s warming chambers kept young birds alive, and wondered why we didn’t do the same for sick human babies. Within a few years his colleague Dr. Bodin proved that incubators save lives, but as we’ve seen over the last 20 years with vaccine hesitancy, science alone isn’t always enough. Incubators needed to go viral. So they signed up an “influencer” to make incubators mainstream. Dr. Couney’s business model would be  unthinkable today. Mothers got free incubator care, with costs paid for by thousands of tourists who paid entrance fees to see odd-looking premature babies in the strange space-age incubator machines. 
 


“Couney’s Child Hatchery” was a wild commercial and medical success and helped catapult incubators into the mainstream, while warming babies become a norm around the world.  Progress sometimes needs all of great ideas, science and PR to scale.

But on the newborn care front, we haven’t “won” the battle to the same extent as with the C-Section. 5000 children under one month old still die every day and 500 of those from neonatal sepsis.

Our boy had lethargy, poor feeding and fever, but hospitals can’t just put all lethargic babies in NICU on all out treatment - especially not in low-income settings. Neonatal sepsis has a diagnosis problem. No single test, or range of clinical features tells us if there’s sepsis. A Center for Global Development team believes this test could be a great life-saving bet, and have proposed a fund of 60 million dollars for any company that develops a working test. For the moment this remains a dream, good tests are far harder to invent than vaccines and treatments.

We would have LOVED one simple test to tell us if our boy was at risk of death, or just struggling a bit to get going. 
 

I am Grateful


At a different time, or right now in a different place our boy would never have been born and might have died twice. I thank the hundreds of innovators and medical staff who took their life saving ideas and made them real. I thank the doctors and nurses who worked with limited resources to help our boy survive and thrive. I thank my mum who struggled with us in those early weeks.

And more than ever I’m grateful for my work with OneDay Health. A friend shared “After you have a kid, your work will feel less important”. But no, it feels more urgent and more important than ever. Even after the worst two weeks of my life, I can’t walk in the shoes of my friends here. I can’t imagine not having two dollars to treat my newborn’s malaria. Or 20 dollars to travel to hospital to give birth. Or even not having $5,000 to cure my child’s heart defect.

But I can imagine doing something today to help these babies live, and there’s never been a better day than today. 

"If you had to choose a moment in history to be born, and you did not know ahead of time who you would be — you didn't know whether you were going to be born into a wealthy family or a poor family, what country you'd be born in, whether you were going to be a man or a woman — if you had to choose blindly what moment you'd want to be born, you'd choose now." - Barrack Obama

item.title: The Featured Page
item.description:
Published on July 28, 2026 10:33 AM GMT

The EA Forum does a lot of things. It’s a place to talk about EA community issues, share jobs, updates from organisations, ask for support with new projects, meet people etc…

All of this is good, but as we all know, not all good things are equally good.

One of the most impactful things the EA Forum does is enable us to have important conversations that could meaningfully shift the focus of funding and talent in the community[1]. As EA grows, I want the Forum to maintain that function, and, indeed, get even better at it.

There will be a number of interventions in this direction in the near future.

The first is the ‘featured page’, launching today. This is a new homepage for the EA Forum which allows us to highlight the posts we (the EA Forum team and moderators, or, for this experimental period: me) think are likely to be the most impactful.

If this works it will a) reward the authors of particularly valuable posts, who will have more readership and have their writing elevated and b) make it easier for readers to find the very best of the EA Forum, however often they turn up.

This page is experimental, we will be collecting data and may revert changes in a few weeks. More details below.

How it works

The regular old frontpage will be re-titled ‘New & Upvoted’. You can access it at the top of the homepage. You will be able to toggle between ‘Featured’ and ‘New & Upvoted’:

 When logged in, clicking on either heading will set it as your default homepage. Next time you visit the site, it's the first page you'll see. 

New comments and posts on the featured page will be highlighted in EA teal. Based on the last month, I'd guess that there will be an average of 6 posts added by the mods every week, and an average of 2 by the Forum audience. Details on how posts are selected is in the 'What goes on the featured page?' section. 

You can choose between card view:

And the more familiar list view:

To switch your default, click on the icon in the top right, above the posts. It looks like this:

What is the featured page for?

Getting (a) more attention for and (b) incentivising the creation of (c) posts which could  meaningfully update (d) an impartial altruist trying to do the most good with their resources.

(a) more attention for: curating a post massively increases the attention that it gets, this will be another lever like that (as long as people find the featured page useful enough).

(b) incentivising the creation of: curation or inclusion in the digest, especially when done by another human being, feels great! The featured page will bestow prestige on posts and therefore authors, and (as long as the criteria are legible) will encourage people to write for it.

(c) meaningfully update: we want people to be changing their minds, for good reasons. The ‘for good reasons’ part depends on the quality of content created by the audience, and selected by the mods.

(d)  an impartial altruist trying to do the most good with their resources: This category contains early career EAs who are still more cause neutral, people in long term EA roles, and the decision-makers and leaders in the movement. 

...well that's the theory. There are also a few other motivating reasons for this page:

  • We get more high quality posts than I can curate, as well as high effort and good posts that fall short of curation, and I'd like to reward them in some way.

  • CEA is growing the EA movement, and more and more text is being AI generated. Both are reasons to expect an incoming wave of low-average quality content. I want to make sure the Forum has the features it needs to deal with this. I don't love the default, where the Forum audience has to search through the slop. Selecting the best is less resource intensive than removing both the worst and the not-great. Hence... Featured page.[2] 

  • Some users we really don't want to lose (i.e. the decision-makers that many authors on the Forum want to influence) want a higher signal version of the Forum. The Featured page will be pre-sorted page, where they won't miss the best ideas coming out of the Forum. 

What goes on the featured page?

The current one sentence explanation at the top of the featured page is:

‘Selected posts to help us answer: how can we do the most good with our resources?’

We’ll be looking to highlight posts which are a) good, and b) could help an impartial altruist meaningfully update their thinking about how to do good with their resources.

We aren't doing an independent consequentialist analysis for the value of each post. The aim is for 'featured' to be a transparent category that the moderation team (and ideally the Forum audience) is aligned on. 

To avoid mod biases, blindspots or unpopular opinions stopping particular kinds of content from making it onto the featured page, we’ll also include ~all[3] posts above 100 karma.[4] 

Plus, you can dm me if you think a post should be featured that isn't - if this happens a lot, we'll make some easier way for users to flag posts as suggested. 

Defining 'featured'

Necessary conditions to be on the featured page

  • The post must be good: engaging, clear and honest.
    • Engaging: i.e. if you post the contents of an arxiv paper rather than a summary, it likely won’t be featured. A featured post should be readable.
    • Clear: not super jargon filled or AI-written to the point of unparseability.
    • Honest: Not clickbait, not using any dishonest persuasive tactics (exaggeration, excessively emotive or angry language, etc…)
  • The post must be ‘on topic’, in other words:
    • It makes an argument or shares information that could change how an impartial altruist prioritises — across causes, within a cause, or in how they deploy their resources, including their career.
      • This is EA, so I’m including a few layers of meta in here; philosophical arguments and quite abstract ones can be included.

    • It is written from or conversant with the effective altruist frame[5].

      • I include ‘conversant with’ to indicate that you don’t have to agree with the EA frame to be on topic. This bullet is just ruling out well written things on EA topics that are scope insensitive, don’t seem impartial etc… (as more and more AI-related stuff will likely be).

What we exclude from the featured page:

Note that ‘community’ ‘announcement’ ‘opportunity to take action’ and ‘organisation update’ posts will be excluded from the >100 karma inclusion. Mods can still feature them manually.

  • Basically all ‘community’ posts — community posts are far from valueless, but my take is that they are incentivised enough already. I wouldn’t want an EA Forum with no community posts, but a good community post already gets a bunch of karma, readers and comments, partially because they are much easier to engage with than an object-level post.
    • For an example of posts that would be featured despite being community, I’d look at some of @Mjreard's posts (like this one), which make or kick off prioritisation arguments, but stay very EA-community-coded.
  • Bare organisation updates — no job postings, RFP postings etc… unless they contain independently good analysis that meets the bar.
  • Newsy and quick to depreciate calls to action: "Do X now!" I want these on the Forum, but the featured page should be more evergreen.
  • Announcements — of a new fellowship, new video, new podcast etc… Again, these are fine to have on the Forum, but not on the featured page, unless they are independently substantive posts.

This is an experiment

The featured page is a pretty big change to how the EA Forum works, and maintaining it will take a lot of curation work. As such, I want to make sure it’s useful before we make it a permanent feature[6].

Based on data we collect over the next few weeks, we’ll decide whether to revert changes, or double down on the featured page. To help us make the right decision, please:

  • Give us some feedback.
  • If you normally are logged in to the EA Forum, make sure you still are. This helps us measure the time spent on featured posts vs other posts.

I would genuinely love your feedback

Please share any takes, concerns, suggestions, or encouragement in the comments, via dm, or through this form (which is optionally anonymous):

Give us feedback

I am fully expecting to tweak the visuals, the inclusion criteria, etc… So don’t feel like anything is out of bounds. I'm ready to debate inclusion criteria in the comments if people are keen. 

Acknowledgements

Massive shout out to @Ollie Etherington for building this page the old fashioned way (typing code himself) and to @Sarah Cheng 🔸 and @Agnes Hasselblad 🔸 for several rounds of mock-ups and feedback. Mistakes or bad decisions are my own. 

 

  1. ^

     Me and @Sarah Cheng 🔸  have been working on the EA Forum’s theory of change a lot this year. I’ll have something to post on this fairly soon, but feel free to ask questions in the comments.

  2. ^

    I'm not saying that everything not on the featured page is bad - that is not the case. In a world where we had to fight a lot more slop, I'd have to find a solution for org updates, community posts etc... as well. 

  3. ^

     Excluding those tagged community, organisation update, announcement and opportunity to take action unless overridden by a mod.

  4. ^

    You might wonder specifically about whether critiques of CEA and the Forum would make it onto the featured page. My guess at this stage is that many wouldn't because they would be firmly community posts (of interest to an EA but unlikely to shift any resources). However, critiques like "The Forum team/CEA is failing in X way, we need an alternative organisation/platform" would make it on if good, because they could in principle affect the flow of resources (they might lead to people funding or founding an alternative). Call me out if you think I'm getting this call wrong. 

  5. ^

     Key aspects of the effective altruist frame to bear in mind: cause neutral, scope sensitive, broadly impartial, welfare maximising.

  6. ^

     Also, if we want to stay relevant in an age of AI writing and Substack popping off (and we do), we need to move fast. I want to be more experimental with the Forum product, without risking the core values of the Forum. Bounded and transparent experiments are a nice way to do that.

(b) incentivising the creation of: curation or inclusion in the digest, especially when done by another human being, feels great! The featured page will bestow prestige on posts and therefore authors, and (as long as the criteria are legible) will encourage people to write for it.

(c) meaningfully update: we want people to be changing their minds, for good reasons. The ‘for good reasons’ part depends on the quality of content created by the audience, and selected by the mods.

(d)  an impartial altruist trying to do the most good with their resources: This category contains early career EAs who are still more cause neutral, people in long term EA roles, and the decision-makers and leaders in the movement. 

...well that's the theory. There are also a few other motivating reasons for this page:

  • We get more high quality posts than I can curate, as well as high effort and good posts that fall short of curation, and I'd like to reward them in some way.

  • CEA is growing the EA movement, and more and more text is being AI generated. Both are reasons to expect an incoming wave of low-average quality content. I want to make sure the Forum has the features it needs to deal with this. I don't love the default, where the Forum audience has to search through the slop. Selecting the best is less resource intensive than removing both the worst and the not-great. Hence... Featured page.[2] 

  • Some users we really don't want to lose (i.e. the decision-makers that many authors on the Forum want to influence) want a higher signal version of the Forum. The Featured page will be pre-sorted page, where they won't miss the best ideas coming out of the Forum. 

What goes on the featured page?

The current one sentence explanation at the top of the featured page is:

‘Selected posts to help us answer: how can we do the most good with our resources?’

We’ll be looking to highlight posts which are a) good, and b) could help an impartial altruist meaningfully update their thinking about how to do good with their resources.

We aren't doing an independent consequentialist analysis for the value of each post. The aim is for 'featured' to be a transparent category that the moderation team (and ideally the Forum audience) is aligned on. 

To avoid mod biases, blindspots or unpopular opinions stopping particular kinds of content from making it onto the featured page, we’ll also include ~all[3] posts above 100 karma.[4] 

Plus, you can dm me if you think a post should be featured that isn't - if this happens a lot, we'll make some easier way for users to flag posts as suggested. 

Defining 'featured'

Necessary conditions to be on the featured page

  • The post must be good: engaging, clear and honest.
    • Engaging: i.e. if you post the contents of an arxiv paper rather than a summary, it likely won’t be featured. A featured post should be readable.
    • Clear: not super jargon filled or AI-written to the point of unparseability.
    • Honest: Not clickbait, not using any dishonest persuasive tactics (exaggeration, excessively emotive or angry language, etc…)
  • The post must be ‘on topic’, in other words:
    • It makes an argument or shares information that could change how an impartial altruist prioritises — across causes, within a cause, or in how they deploy their resources, including their career.
      • This is EA, so I’m including a few layers of meta in here; philosophical arguments and quite abstract ones can be included.

    • It is written from or conversant with the effective altruist frame[5].

      • I include ‘conversant with’ to indicate that you don’t have to agree with the EA frame to be on topic. This bullet is just ruling out well written things on EA topics that are scope insensitive, don’t seem impartial etc… (as more and more AI-related stuff will likely be).

What we exclude from the featured page:

Note that ‘community’ ‘announcement’ ‘opportunity to take action’ and ‘organisation update’ posts will be excluded from the >100 karma inclusion. Mods can still feature them manually.

  • Basically all ‘community’ posts — community posts are far from valueless, but my take is that they are incentivised enough already. I wouldn’t want an EA Forum with no community posts, but a good community post already gets a bunch of karma, readers and comments, partially because they are much easier to engage with than an object-level post.
    • For an example of posts that would be featured despite being community, I’d look at some of @Mjreard's posts (like this one), which make or kick off prioritisation arguments, but stay very EA-community-coded.
  • Bare organisation updates — no job postings, RFP postings etc… unless they contain independently good analysis that meets the bar.
  • Newsy and quick to depreciate calls to action: "Do X now!" I want these on the Forum, but the featured page should be more evergreen.
  • Announcements — of a new fellowship, new video, new podcast etc… Again, these are fine to have on the Forum, but not on the featured page, unless they are independently substantive posts.

This is an experiment

The featured page is a pretty big change to how the EA Forum works, and maintaining it will take a lot of curation work. As such, I want to make sure it’s useful before we make it a permanent feature[6].

Based on data we collect over the next few weeks, we’ll decide whether to revert changes, or double down on the featured page. To help us make the right decision, please:

  • Give us some feedback.
  • If you normally are logged in to the EA Forum, make sure you still are. This helps us measure the time spent on featured posts vs other posts.

I would genuinely love your feedback

Please share any takes, concerns, suggestions, or encouragement in the comments, via dm, or through this form (which is optionally anonymous):

Give us feedback

I am fully expecting to tweak the visuals, the inclusion criteria, etc… So don’t feel like anything is out of bounds. I'm ready to debate inclusion criteria in the comments if people are keen. 

Acknowledgements

Massive shout out to @Ollie Etherington for building this page the old fashioned way (typing code himself) and to @Sarah Cheng 🔸 and @Agnes Hasselblad 🔸 for several rounds of mock-ups and feedback. Mistakes or bad decisions are my own.

  2. ^

    I'm not saying that everything not on the featured page is bad - that is not the case. In a world where we had to fight a lot more slop, I'd have to find a solution for org updates, community posts etc... as well. 

  3. ^

  4. ^

    You might wonder specifically about whether critiques of CEA and the Forum would make it onto the featured page. My guess at this stage is that many wouldn't because they would be firmly community posts (of interest to an EA but unlikely to shift any resources). However, critiques like "The Forum team/CEA is failing in X way, we need an alternative organisation/platform" would make it on if good, because they could in principle affect the flow of resources (they might lead to people funding or founding an alternative). Call me out if you think I'm getting this call wrong. 

  5. ^

  6. ^
