item.description:
Published on July 28, 2026 4:29 PM GMT

Written by Lucas Moore (Senior Partnerships Manager), Giving What We Can for the Effective Giving Summit 2026. Published with some elements redacted.

This memo provides a high-level overview of the effective giving landscape as of May 2026. It builds on the memo we wrote for last year's summit (later published with some elements redacted) and is based largely on the 2026 EG pulse survey and money moved sheet (not public). Please leave a comment if you'd like us to clarify anything. All figures are in USD.

Background

The effective giving ecosystem is an interdependent network of >70 organisations directing philanthropic resources to where they can do the most good, guided by principles such as cost-effectiveness, cause prioritisation and counterfactual impact. Within the ecosystem, some organisations identify high-impact opportunities (evaluators) and others fundraise for them (fundraisers). Many do both.

Key updates

  • Money moved by the ecosystem (not public)[1] grew by ~60% between 2024 and 2025, from ~1.2B to ~2B money moved

    • The bulk of that growth came from Coefficient Giving and GiveWell

      • Coefficient Giving: stable at ~650M since 2022, grew ~50% to ~1B in 2025

      • GiveWell: stable at ~200M since 2021, grew ~100% to ~490M in 2025

    • Significant growth also from Founders Pledge, Navigation Fund and Giving Green

      • Founders Pledge continued its YoY trajectory: ~25M (2022) to ~80M (2023) to ~140M (2024) to ~180M (2025)

      • Navigation Fund cemented itself as a major funder (moving 10-100M per year)

      • Giving Green emerged as a major fundraiser: ~30M in 2025[2], up from ~10M in 2024

    • Though smaller in absolute terms, the rest of the ecosystem grew at similar relative levels

      • Excluding Coefficient Giving and GiveWell, the ecosystem grew by ~50% from ~340M to ~490M

      • Total money raised by national fundraising orgs grew by ~45% from ~44M to ~64M

        • Effektiv Spenden (DACH) showed that the national fundraising model has not (yet) hit a ceiling in any market: ~40% growth (from ~25M to ~35M)[3]

      • The number of organisations moving more than 1M grew from ~22 to ~24

  • Anthropic will likely represent the largest expansion in funding the EG ecosystem has yet seen
    • Many people at Anthropic are considering giving effectively
      • Many among the co-founders, leadership, and early employees are GWWC pledgers and/or have strong personal connections to organisations and people active in the EG ecosystem
    • At the company’s ~1T May 2026 valuation the co-founder giving pledges alone would have been worth ~15B each, ~100B combined (~30x what Coefficient Giving has given away in its entire history)
      • The 7 co-founders have all pledged ~80% of their wealth and each likely holds ~2% of the company (although estimates vary)
    • Anthropic is also likely to produce a wider set of (smaller but still very large) major donors (likely adding billions, if not 10s of billions, more in funding)
      • For much of the company’s existence, employees have been able to pledge 25-50% of their equity to 501c3 nonprofits with Anthropic matching between 1:1 and 3:1
    • The speed at which this funding will enter the ecosystem is a big uncertainty
      • Prediction markets currently put the chance of an IPO before 2027 at ~70%
      • Regardless of IPO timing, secondary sales and further private rounds will likely start bringing significant amounts of funding online earlier
      • That said, there is obviously uncertainty both whether and when this money will materialise and whether and to what extent donors will elect to spend it using effective giving principles
  • Other notable updates
    • Coefficient Giving has started to diversify away from sole reliance on Good Ventures (Dustin and Cari) and more than doubled money moved from new partners
    • The Centre For Effective Altruism acquired Effective Altruism Funds
    • GWWC published a new round of evaluations of evaluators and now relies on
      • GiveWell (2025 report)
      • Animal Charity Evaluators' Movement Grants (2024 report)
      • Effective Altruism Funds' Animal Welfare Fund (2023 report)
      • Longview Philanthropy's Emerging Challenges Fund (2023 report)
      • Effective Altruism Funds' Long-Term Future Fund (2023 report)
      • (Re-)evaluations in 2026 are planned in global catastrophic risks, animal welfare, and potentially democracy/institution building

Overview of the ecosystem

  • Database of organisations (evaluators and fundraisers)
    • >70 effective giving orgs
    • Most are <5 FTE. Other than that ~20 are >5 FTE. The largest by headcount are Coefficient Giving, GiveWell and Founders Pledge (all >50 FTE)
  • Database of publicly accessible evaluators
    • The public-facing impact-focused charity evaluation and grantmaking field is still (very) small. Only 9 evaluators have at ≥3 FTE on evaluation and/or grantmaking: Coefficient Giving, GiveWell, Founders Pledge, Centre For Effective Altruism (having acquired EA Funds), Animal Charity Evaluators, Longview Philanthropy, Navigation Fund, Giving Green and Happier Lives Institute
    • No impact-focused evaluator exists for meta charities (i.e. charitable projects working one level removed from direct impact), pandemics or AI risks apart from Founders Pledge. Although, a few grantmakers do operate in those spaces (Coefficient Giving, Navigation Fund, Astralis, Macroscopic Ventures, Longview Philanthropy, Centre For Effective Altruism (having acquired EA Funds), Sentinel Bio, etc.)
    • Rethink Priorities launched a Cross-Cause Fund (the first of its kind) to pool donations from multiple donors and allocate them to high-impact giving funds across cause areas, such as global health, animal welfare, and global catastrophic risk reduction
  • Effective Giving Global Coordination and Incubation
    • In May 2023 Giving What We Can hired Lucas Moore (me) to support coordination and collaboration in the global EG ecosystem, including by organising the annual Effective Giving Summit
    • Following the 2026 EG Summit, Giving What We Can decided to continue providing three public goods to the effective giving ecosystem, and these are the only ecosystem work that Giving What We Can should take on for now:
      • Convening: the EG Summit and Evaluators Forum
      • Information node: the ecosystem annual pulse survey and associated update (this post), money moved (not public) and total number of donors (not public) sheets, ecosystem overview, and evaluators database.
      • Quality control: evaluating evaluators, impact evaluation toolkit.
    • See Giving What We Can‘s public ecosystem strategy.
  • Where operational funding comes from
    • Coefficient Giving is the largest single funder of meta charities
      • ~7M/yr budget for EG orgs, from their career/EG focused portfolio of ~10M/yr
      • In 2026 their career/EG program budget has increased to ~30M/yr (unclear what % will go to EG orgs)
    • Meta Charity Funders (funding circle) is a key funder for smaller and early-stage meta charities like EG orgs
    • See other funding sources

How much money is moved to high-impact destinations[4]

  • 1 organisation moved >1B (for the first time)
    • ~1B: Coefficient Giving
  • 3 organisations moved >100M (same as 2024)
    • ~1B: ^ see above ^
    • ~490M: GiveWell
    • ~180M: Founders Pledge
  • ~12 organisations moved >10M (up from ~10 in 2024)
    • >100M: ^ see above ^
    • ~30M: Effektiv Spenden (DACH), Survival and Flourishing Fund, Longview Philanthropy, Giving What We Can, Giving Green
    • >10M: The Life You Can Save, Astralis Foundation, Centre For Effective Altruism (via EA Funds, mainly through Giving What We Can’s donation infrastructure), Navigation Fund
  • ~24 organisations moved >1M in 2025 (up from ~22 in 2024)
    • >10M: ^ see above ^
    • >5M: Doneer Effectief (Netherlands), Sentinel Bio, Animal Charity Evaluators
    • >1M: EA Australia, Gi Effektivt (Norway), RC Forward (Canada), Ultra Philanthropy, Ayuda Efectiva (Spain), Ge Effektivt (Sweden), One For The World, EA New Zealand, Giving Multiplier

  • For some organisations (e.g. Ark Philanthropy, Effective Institutions Project, Macrosopic Ventures, AI Safety Tactical Opportunities Fund[5], etc.) we don't have a good sense of the amount of money moved

Donors giving through the ecosystem

  • A rough estimate of donors giving through EG orgs suggests the number grew by ~24% between 2024 and 2025, from ~69k to ~86k[6]

  • The donor distribution is generally heavy-tailed with a small share of donors accounting for a large % of total giving across ~all EG orgs

Where money goes

  • A rough look at this (aided by Claude) indicated that the money moved by the EG ecosystem (not public) went to the following cause areas:
    • ~50% to global health
    • ~30% to global catastrophic risk reduction (up from ~20% in 2024)
    • ~10% to animal welfare
    • ~5% to climate change mitigation
    • (the rest is unknown or a bit harder to categorise: ~5%)
  • Coefficient Giving and GiveWell dominate the effective giving space (~80% of money moved), and their cause area distribution may not reflect the (future) distribution of donors in the broad EG community as it grows (e.g. the potential influx of Anthropic donors may change this, even when many of them may give through Coefficient Giving and GiveWell as well).
    • GiveWell moved 100% to global health in 2025
    • Coefficient Giving moved roughly to the following cause areas for 2025
      • ~35% to global health
      • ~50% to global catastrophic risk reduction
      • ~10% to animal welfare
      • (the rest is a bit harder to categorise: ~5%)
  • Our current rough estimate (excluding Coefficient Giving):
    • ~70% to global health (up from ~60% in 2024)
    • ~10% to global catastrophic risk reduction (down from ~20% in 2024)
    • ~5% to animal welfare
    • ~10% to climate change mitigation
    • (the rest is unknown or a bit harder to categorise: ~5%)
  • Our current rough estimate (excluding Coefficient Giving and GiveWell):
    • ~40% to global health
    • ~20% to global catastrophic risk reduction (down from 30% in 2024)
    • ~10% to animal welfare
    • ~20% to climate change mitigation
    • (the rest is unknown or a bit harder to categorise: ~10%)

 

  1. ^

     For the purposes of this overview, "money moved to high-impact destinations" refers to funds donated directly to an organisation's accounts by a donor, with a high-impact destination (i.e. one recommended or granted to by an impact-focused evaluator). Some organisations also move money to destinations not considered high-impact, but these funds are not included for our purposes e.g. in 2025 Founders Pledge moved a total of ~300M, but only ~180M is considered high-impact. This also excludes a few organisations that did not share their money moved figures for 2025 with us, e.g. Ark Philanthropy, Effective Institutions Project, Macrosopic Ventures, AI Safety Tactical Opportunities Fund, FarmKind.

  2. ^

     Giving Green received a ~50M donation from an anonymous donor in 2025, however when they receive very large gifts (~20M or more) without an indication of donor intent or multi-year commitments, they may choose to spread grantmaking over two years to ensure that they have money available for highly impactful future opportunities. This is what they’ve done in 2025 such that they’ve only reported ~30M.

  3. ^

     In 2024 it was unclear whether the model could keep growing past a level of market penetration. E.g. Effektiv Spenden (DACH) had plateaued at ~20-25M for a couple of years. The 2025 growth of Effektiv Spenden (DACH) of ~40% has further validated the model and we have not (yet) found a ceiling for how far it can scale.

  4. ^

     Again, for the purposes of this overview, "money moved to high-impact destinations" refers to funds donated directly to an organisation's accounts by a donor, with a high-impact destination (i.e. one recommended or granted to by an impact-focused evaluator). Some organisations also move money to destinations not considered high-impact, but these funds are not included for our purposes e.g. in 2025 Founders Pledge moved a total of ~300M, but only ~180M is considered high-impact. This excludes a few organisations that did not share their money moved figures for 2025 with us, e.g. Ark Philanthropy, Effective Institutions Project, Macrosopic Ventures, AI Safety Tactical Opportunities Fund, FarmKind.

  5. ^

     The AI Safety Tactical Opportunities Fund is likely still moving >10M, but we haven't been able to confirm for 2025.

  6. ^

     Self-reported figures from the 2025 and 2026 pulse surveys give a rough sense of how many people are giving in accordance with EG principles. These should be understood as order-of-magnitude estimates only because the same individual can give through multiple orgs, so the totals may overstate distinct individuals, and not all organisations reported on this (though the largest few retail fundraisers did).

item.title: GWWC’s effective giving ecosystem strategy 2026/27
item.description:
Published on July 28, 2026 4:49 PM GMT

Written by Sjir Hoeijmakers (CEO) and Lucas Moore (Senior Partnerships Manager), Giving What We Can following the Effective Giving Summit 2026.

The core proposition

GWWC provides three public goods to the effective giving ecosystem, and these are the only ecosystem work we should take on for now:

  1. Convening: the EG Summit and Evaluators Forum
  2. Information node: the ecosystem annual pulse survey and associated update, money moved (not public) and total number of donors (not public) sheets, ecosystem overview, and evaluators database.
  3. Quality control: evaluating evaluators, impact evaluation toolkit.

We are a key coordinator, but not the only one, and don’t aim to be the exclusive provider of these three goods either. We provide them because we are uniquely well-placed to, and we invite others to contribute to these goods alongside us and to build the public goods we are not building.

Why this scope

We considered the full range from substantially expanding our coordination role (up to incubating or spinning out a broader coordinating body), and dropping GWWC’s coordination work entirely. We landed deliberately at a mid-point where we feel currently able to create the most value.

Why not less. These three functions provide a lot of value, both for the ecosystem as a whole and for GWWC’s own strategy. They enable GWWC to take a role strongly aligned with our values (e.g. alliance mentality, proactive integrity), and to represent and promote these values in the ecosystem. And they are relatively low-lift for us because we already do them and have the assets in house. In the longer term, we think a separate organisation could house some if not all of these goods, and we might decide to spin them out at some point (see below), but in the meantime we are best positioned to house them.

Why not more. We are a growing organisation with an ambitious strategy that requires focus, and so we cannot take on every public good the ecosystem needs. Taking on more, particularly work less aligned with our core strategy or competencies, would dilute both the quality of our core and our public goods work.

In some ways, this is a solidification of a direction we were already heading in last year: more clearly bounding and specializing our “ecosystem coordination and incubation” role in a way that plays to GWWC’s key strengths and creates space for others to fill the gaps we don’t think we are best positioned to fill.

Why these three specifically

The same elements run through all of them: we already do them reasonably well; we have the relevant people, expertise, and trust in house; and no one else is currently better positioned. For other public goods, there is much less of a comparative advantage for GWWC to pick these up.

  • Convening, and in particular the EG Summit, has clear traction and value, based on attendance, feedback and concrete follow-ups. We have the in-house expertise and trust of other organisations to host the Summit, built up over the past four years. Furthermore, it enables us to lead by example in values we think are important for effective giving beyond GWWC, and create the conditions for a high-quality, collaborative, transparent, and high-integrity ecosystem.
    1. For the Summit, one slight update in approach is that we’d like to take on (even) more of a facilitative rather than agenda setting role, particularly in areas where we have less expertise or context, such as (U)HNW advising e.g. one takeaway from the 2026 Summit is that most of the value was in bringing together the right people and allowing them to self-organize in meeting (in 1-1s and small groups) and sharing their thoughts (in memos), and the least value was in us trying to curate content around topics of interest to the group, but where we had little context on. Relatedly, we’re planning to ask (even) more input from various key stakeholders in the ecosystem on how to best curate the Summit invite list, as we will not have all the relevant context in house.
    2. For 2027, the only meeting we’ll likely host beyond the Summit is an Evaluators Forum. The main reason is again that we seem particularly well-positioned to do this, both through evaluating evaluators and through having a stake in the evaluation and grantmaking field improving broadly (rather than in a particular cause). For other potential convenings of sub-spaces (e.g. (U)HNW advisory, broad-base fundraising) we think there are other actors who are better suited to host these (e.g. European national fundraising orgs are already exploring hosting a convening later this year).
  • The information node is low-lift and supports our convening. To keep this so, we’ll limit our work here to a few high-value ecosystem-wide pieces we’re mostly already providing, such as the annual pulse survey, money moved sheet, and total number of donors sheet. To play to our comparative advantage, we explicitly don’t aim to be the information node on every topic, e.g. we are less well positioned to do this in the (U)HNW advisory sub-space.
  • Quality control through evaluating evaluators and impact evaluation is work we need to do as part of our core strategy regardless. Proactively sharing it is low-hanging fruit and exemplifies our values of alliance mentality, proactive integrity and mission accountability in the ecosystem. We invite other organisations to collaborate and compete on evaluating evaluators and funds as there’s currently a larger evaluation gap than only we can fill, and we believe this will increase quality of evaluations longer-term.

What we are explicitly NOT doing

  • We are not the ecosystem's only coordinator or strategic leader: we provide three specific goods, and don’t claim a broader mandate.
  • We are not building other public goods: we help others build them through the three goods we provide; we don't build them ourselves.
  • We are not claiming exclusivity: we welcome other evaluators, other conveners, other information-holders, and collaborate and compete gladly.

We name these boundaries partly so others feel actively invited to fill the gaps we leave.

Other public goods we'd like to see

We’ve identified a few plausibly high-value (categories of) public goods that we would love others to build, as we don’t think we are well-positioned to do this:

  • Cause prioritisation research
  • Convenings in the broad fundraising and (U)HNW space
  • Shared standards and coordination among meta funders
  • Talent recruitment and pipeline coordination and improvement
  • Filling cause area gaps in the grantmaking and evaluation space
  • Best practices and template sharing in advising and fundraising (we might consider this in the future in the evaluation and grantmaking space, as a natural extension of evaluating evaluators)
  • Donor coordination among (U)HNW advisors
  • Crisis response / Rapid reallocation infrastructure
  • Formalized EG standard-setting and accreditation

By default, we will contribute to these being built only through the three public goods we provide, and in particular through helping to surface gaps and connecting the right people via convening and being an information node.

What would change this conclusion

We plan to re-evaluate our coordination activities at least every year immediately following the EG Summit, as this is when we’ll have the best information position to do so. We can already indicate a few triggers that could change our conclusions on specific goods or all three of them if they were to materialize:

  1. A dedicated, independent coordination organisation is founded
    1. We don’t think there currently is enough work to justify such an organisation, and there are various challenges with founding one, but if one were to exist we could see us spinning out some or all of these functions to that organisation.
  2. A better-positioned party emerges
    1. If another organisation steps forward to provide any of these functions and does so in a plausibly better quality way and/or in a way that replaces rather than complements our work, we would consider winding it down.
  3. Significant conflicts of interest emerge
    1. If at any point conflicts of interest emerge that are significant, e.g. there is a need for us to evaluate one of our funders as an evaluator, this might prompt us to spin out certain functions.
  4. The work is no longer plausibly competitive with our core strategy
    1. If we find on further evaluation that any of these three public goods is (much) less valuable or more costly than we currently expect, e.g. future EG Summits show lower returns and/or significantly larger resource needs, this could prompt winding down.
  5. There’s a strong case for a new public good that we’re not yet providing
    1. We’re open to pitches of public goods that seem highly valuable and we’re well-positioned to provide, though we have a very high bar for taking up any more such work given costs of reduced focus.
  6. Key personnel  leave GWWC
    1. Part of the case for us providing these goods is our current in-house context and trust, and a large part of that is held by the authors of this post (Lucas and Sjir), so if either of us were to leave this would cause reconsideration.
  7. The ecosystem no longer wants GWWC to provide these
    1. If for some reason we lose trust or lose uptake from (key organisations in) the ecosystem in some other way, this could cause us to wind down or find a more suitable organisation to provide these goods.
